summary: The paper measures the 1999 single-algorithm cross-validated filter (5-fold out-of-fold logistic regression, drop disagreements, refit) on digits and breast cancer under 20% and 40% symmetric label noise, with 5 seeds. It reports that dropped samples are mostly flipped (precision well above the realized noise rate, high recall), that the refit model beats plain logistic regression on digits and on breast cancer at 40% (with large variance and only 22% recovery), and that an untuned MLP degrades much more. It is candid that this is a small measurement study with no comparison to other filters.
strengths: Honest scoping: the paper says it is not a new method, states what was not run (class-dependent noise, other filters, ablations, MLP tuning), and ties the claims to the cells where they hold.
Paired design over seeds (shared split, noise draw and folds), a clean test split that is never corrupted, and the filter's drop precision reported against the realized noise rate.
Mixed results are reported plainly: the non-significant breast cancer 20% gain, the 22% recovery and large sd at 40%, the clean-label cost, and the 5x fit time.

weaknesses.issue: The headline comparison is against a weak baseline, and the only strong-ish alternative is an untuned MLP that the paper itself says is not a fair comparison. There is no control that separates 'targeting flipped labels' from 'dropping about 30-50% of the data'. Without a random-drop control (same drop count), an oracle drop (remove exactly the flipped labels), or a regularized logistic regression (smaller C), the accuracy gain cannot be attributed to the out-of-fold disagreement. The discussion concedes this.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add the cheap controls the data allow: random drop at the same rate, oracle drop, and logistic regression with a few values of C. If they cannot be run, soften the causal wording ('why disagreement marks a flipped label', 'finds most of the flipped labels') and state in the abstract that the gain is not isolated.

weaknesses.issue: The precision claim is inconsistent and its test is not meaningful. The Table 2 caption and column report a t-test of precision against 50%, but Sec. 4 says no test against a fixed level is reported, and the stated baseline for a random drop is the realized noise rate (~20/40%). On digits the 'lift' is relative to 9-class symmetric noise, where 50% is not a natural null. The text also refers to a 'lift' and a 'loss column' in Table 2 that do not exist in the table.
weaknesses.suggestion: Replace the 50% test with precision minus realized noise rate (paired over seeds), or drop the p column. Add the realized noise rate, lift and accuracy-loss columns that the text cites. Fix the contradiction between Sec. 4 and the caption.

weaknesses.issue: The evidence is thin for the claims made. There are 5 seeds, two small, nearly linearly separable datasets, and about a dozen uncorrected tests; paired t-tests with n=5 are fragile. The paper itself calls the p-values descriptive, yet the abstract and intro use 'clearly beats' and 'significant'. The breast cancer 40% cell has sd 9.0 points and 22% recovery, and the text says the cause is unknown, even though the data (per-seed realized noise, recall) could be checked.
weaknesses.suggestion: Report effect sizes with CIs (already in Fig. 2) and avoid 'significant' wording, or raise the seed count (these models are cheap; 20-50 seeds or repeated splits are feasible). Show per-seed values for breast cancer 40% and relate gain to per-seed recall/noise realization instead of saying the cause is unknown.

weaknesses.issue: The 'recovered share' is a ratio with a small or noisy denominator. It is reported as a mean over seeds, which is unstable (the paper admits this). The 22% vs 66-78% contrast carries much of the 'partial support' narrative, but the 40% breast cancer logistic regression has sd 9.4, so a per-seed ratio can be erratic. The ratio of means and the mean of ratios may differ.
weaknesses.suggestion: State whether recovery is a ratio of means or a mean of per-seed ratios, and report it with a bootstrap CI or give the pooled version.

weaknesses.issue: The clean-label 'cost below resolution' claim is an absence-of-evidence argument. Digits shows -0.2 pt and breast cancer ~0.1 pt, but 5 seeds cannot show equivalence (the paper says so), and the abstract still presents it as a finding. Also, the filter drops about 3.5% of clean digits samples, which is a real cost on larger or harder data.
weaknesses.suggestion: Phrase it as 'no detectable cost' with the CI, or run an equivalence test (TOST) with a stated margin.

weaknesses.issue: The MLP comparison does not support its framing. The MLP is untuned, has no early stopping, and is not trained on the filtered set. Including it as a headline baseline in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 and the contribution list invites the reading that filtering beats nonlinear models, which the text then disclaims. It is 'a model with 100% training fit on noisy labels', not a noise-robust baseline.
weaknesses.suggestion: Either train the MLP on the filtered set and with early stopping/weight decay, or move the MLP to a single sentence and remove it from the teaser and contributions.

weaknesses.issue: Framing and presentation: the paper's title ('Out-of-Fold Filtering of Symmetric Label Noise for a Linear Model: A Small Measurement Study') is a measurement study of a 1999 method with no baselines among other filters (confident learning, which is available in a few lines). This limits the contribution at the workshop. The Sec. 3 argument ('why disagreement may mark a flipped label') is informal. A simple expected-precision bound (given symmetric noise rate and the model's clean error rate) could be compared with the measured precision.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add confident learning (cleanlab) with the same logistic regression as one extra row, and a short analytic expected-precision sanity check. Also fix the minor text-level mismatches: 'recovers a minor share' vs 'about a fifth', and the 'in every seed' wins claim versus the sd shown in Fig. 2.

questions: What is the random-drop and oracle-drop accuracy at the same drop count, and how much of the digits gain does each explain?
Why is precision lower at 40% than at 20% on breast cancer but higher on digits? Is the breast cancer 40% instability driven by seeds where the first-fold models are themselves corrupted?
Does the gain hold with a tuned C (e.g. smaller C as implicit regularization) for plain logistic regression?
Are the 5 seeds repeated splits, and is the noise draw independent across noise rates?
What happens with class-dependent noise, where the argument in Sec. 3 predicts failure?
